questions.question: A function needs to react to exactly one Boolean question — is a number negative or not — with no other cases. Which of the four forms reads best, and why?
options: case...of, because it is the most general form and general is always safest
if...then...else, because there is exactly one Boolean condition and exactly two outcomes — precisely what it is built for
Guards, because guards are required whenever a Boolean test is involved
Pattern matching, because every decision in Haskell should use patterns
questions.explanation: The comparison table above states this directly: if...then...else reads best when there are exactly two outcomes decided by one Boolean condition. Reaching for a more general tool than the decision actually needs makes the code harder to read, not more powerful.
optionFeedback: case...of being more general does not make it the better choice here — matching the tool to the shape of the decision is the whole point of this chapter, and a single Boolean split is if-then-else's exact use case.
Correct — one condition, two outcomes, is exactly the shape if...then...else was designed for.
Guards are for a sequence of several Boolean tests on the same argument, typically ranges; a single yes/no question does not need that machinery.
Pattern matching chooses on shape or literal value, not on an arbitrary Boolean test — 'is negative' is not a shape, it's a condition, which points at if-then-else or a single-guard function instead.
